newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/ Xerox after earnings.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/ Xerox after earnings.

text.p: Xerox Corp puts and calls options saw heavy traffic after the stock plunged on news of the firm's dismal earnings, traders said.

"The stock looks really ugly," said Rod Jamieson, vice president of option strategy at EVEREN Securities. The stock topped the New York Stock Exchange's most actives list, losing 8-1/8 to 48-7/8 on hefty turnover of 19,516,700 shares.

The stock's plunge triggered, apart from obvious put buying, various hedging trades, traders said. There was also some bottom-fishing as the gap between today's and Thursday's ranges was huge and appeared waiting to be filled.
"Options may have been used to reduce some of the risk of the block sales," said Michael Schwartz, a managing director of Oppenheimer & Co.

Option volume was well above normal levels with heavy traffic on both put and call sides. November 50 calls was the busiest contract, with 3,926 lots trading. On the put side, November 55 puts had turnover of 1,633.
Schwartz noted that volume in the November 55 puts had totalled 1,258 lots on Thursday, with most of it contributing to a 1,137-contract increase in open interest to 1,629.

"There may have been some front-running," he said. "It looks like eleven hundred out of the 1,258 were new commitments and therefore would lead me to conclude they were related to anticipation of these earnings."
Xerox third quarter earnings came in at $0.68 per share against analysts' average estimates of $0.82 against $0.70 a year earlier.

Illustrating how such a stock price movement can boost option prices, the premium on October 55 puts, whose trading ended today for expiration on Saturday, jumped 48-fold to 6 from Thursday's 1/8 close on volume of 449 contracts.
The contract, which had seemed certain to expire worthless only a day before, suddenly became deep in-the-money overnight with very short life to maturity, traders said.
Elsewhere, the options market was dominated by roll-over of positions due to the expiration of October contracts.
Schwartz said a lot of call options used for buy-writes, or covered calls, were being rolled over. Buy-writes are combinations of long stock and short call positions.
"It's more economical to roll over than to let them (calls) be exercised and pay the stock commission as opposed to option commissions," Schwartz said.
